Theme

School & learning · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

theory noun

the principles of a subject, as against practice

also in theory, theoretical, theoretically, theory and practice, in principle

classical

Caes. BG 4.1.6: ratiō atque ūsus bellī

ratiō, ratiōnis f.

noun, third declension

theory, the principles (as against practice)

Latin sets ratiō or scientia against ūsus, practice (Caes. BG 4.1.6; Cic. Rep. 1.2).

Other words

  • scientia, scientiae f. — knowledge without practice

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 1.2: scientiā tamen ipsā tenērī potest

    See knowledge.

  • ars, artis f. — an art, its rules and principles

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 1.2: ars quidem, cum eā nōn ūtāre

    See subject.

  • theōria, theōriae f. — theory, speculation

    noun, first declension · also used · late Latin · Hier. in Ezech. 12.40.4 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. practical: theory

    Cicero writes it in Greek (Att. 12.6.1: Lewis & Short); in Latin from Jerome on. Morgan–Owens gives it for theory as against practice.

Examples

  • Nec vērō habēre virtūtem satis est quasi artem aliquam, nisi ūtāre; etsī ars quidem, cum eā nōn ūtāre, scientiā tamen ipsā tenērī potest, virtūs in ūsū suī tōta posita est

    Nor is it enough to have virtue as one has some art, unless you use it; for an art, even when you do not use it, can still be held by knowledge alone, but virtue lies wholly in its useCic. Rep. 1.2

  • Sīc neque agrī cultūra nec ratiō atque ūsus bellī intermittitur.

    So neither farming nor the theory and practice of war is ever broken off.Caes. BG 4.1.6

See also theory, knowledge, experience, subject.
